source.title: High-dimensional dynamics of generalization error in neural networks
source.authors: Madhu S. Advani; Andrew M. Saxe; H. Sompolinsky

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes generalization and training-error dynamics across model sizes, training times, and sample-to-parameter ratios using analytical solutions and simulations, rather than reproducing the original sources' method.
record.gate_note: The paper's own analytical and simulated error results are included. Results it attributes to other studies are not included. Values available only in plots are not transcribed as numerical values.
record.test_reason: Exact random-matrix solutions for linear students plus simulations of random-feature and two-layer ReLU students and MNIST. These trace test error against sample/parameter ratio, model size and training time. They show a test-error spike at the interpolation point (α = 1, or free parameters = P) that falls on both sides. This is a different method aimed at the same question; the study is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Overtraining and long-time test error are worst when effective free parameters equal samples, and fall on both sides. In the linear case, the late-stopping error diverges at α = 1. Early stopping plus small initial weights nearly matches optimal L2 regularization. Large nonlinear models generalize well, even without early stopping when SNR is high, owing to a frozen subspace and a widening eigengap.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random-matrix analysis and student-teacher simulations, including nonlinear networks and MNIST; it does not reproduce the original sources' method.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on sample-to-parameter ratio, signal-to-noise ratio, initialization size, model size, whether one or both layers are trained, training duration, and early stopping. The MNIST overtraining peak is less distinct with only 5000 epochs and a maximum model size of 1740.

fits_no_version.finding: Overtraining (late minus early-stopped error) peaks where trainable parameters match samples, including on MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gap between long-time and optimally early-stopped test error peaks at the interpolation threshold and shrinks on both sides.

record.problems: The nonlinear size-sweep findings are largely reported qualitatively in the text; plotted values are not available as text. MNIST training was limited to 5000 epochs and a maximum model size of 1740, making its overtraining peak less distinct. The paper notes that most nonlinear experiments use networks with at most one hidden layer.

untested.parts: Any second descent over training time; deep nonlinear networks.
Model classes beyond linear regression, random-feature ReLU and two-layer ReLU nets (e.g. trees, kernels).
A single complexity measure predicting peak location across epochs, size and samples. The paper only places the peak at parameter count = P.
Multiple or triple peaks. Whether optimally tuned explicit regularization removes the model-size peak.
Deep (more than one hidden layer) nonlinear networks; modern architectures.

missing.what: Overtraining peak magnitude grows approximately proportionally to inverse SNR across SNR settings.
MNIST: even at long training times the best model was the largest tested, i.e. long-time error falls past the interpolation size.
Fixed-first-layer long-time test error diverges at Nh = P (Fig. 6F middle), a direct size-wise peak in test error.
Generalization error vs α for different initial weight norms; large initial weights worsen error in the α<1 regime.

record.verdict_notes: This 2017 paper predates the original sources but shows model-wise and sample-wise peaks at interpolation under long training. The peaks vanish under optimal early stopping. r7 and r9 were upgraded to observed for V1 using the Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 6 text. V2 is only a classical single overtraining hump. The V5 link (peak at parameter count = P) is too narrow to count as a test.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not establish a fall-rise-fall test-error curve across model sizes under a common fixed training schedule; some size-sweep findings concern optimal early stopping or the amount of overtraining.
The reported training-time curves show a decrease followed by worsening or convergence; the paper does not report a subsequent second decrease.
The sample-size result is for the shallow linear student-teacher setting with the stated random-matrix assumptions, not a broad range of nonlinear or real-world settings.
The study examines shallow linear networks and minimally deep nonlinear networks, including a two-layer MNIST setting; it does not test arbitrary model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across model size, epochs, and sample size.

The study varies signal-to-noise ratio and compares early stopping with optimally tuned L2 regularization in a shallow linear setting. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimal regularization removes a model-size peak.
The paper does not test whether recounting complexity using an effective parameter count converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network
rows.operation_detail: Varied the sample-to-parameter ratio α = P/N and evaluated generalization error at several training times.
rows.measure: Generalization error versus sample-to-parameter ratio α
rows.value: The text reports a clear spike near α = 1; it identifies α = 1 as the point where overtraining is worst.
rows.note: Here N is fixed and α changes with the number of samples. The result therefore bears on sample-size changes, not a model-size sweep.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network
rows.operation_detail: Measured generalization error during full-batch gradient descent.
rows.value: The text says the curve exhibits overfitting; at α = 1/2, zero-eigenvalue directions are never learned and contribute finite error without overtraining.
rows.note: The reported dynamics do not describe a second descent after the error worsens.
rows.check: Fall then rise or convergence only; the exact solution shows no second descent.

source_check.correct: V2 state: absent. Generalization error initially improves, then worsens toward its late-time value; no second temporal descent.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.1, Fig. 2B caption; Section 2.2 opening paragraph.
source_check.problem: Ordinary overtraining without the defining second descent does not establish partial epoch-wise double descent.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network

rows.check: Fall then rise (divergence) only; no second descent.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network
rows.operation_detail: Compared predicted generalization and training-error dynamics with simulations over 20 trials.
rows.measure: Generalization and training error over training time
rows.value: The simulations show excellent agreement with the theoretical predictions; generalization error exhibits overtraining, especially at α = 1.
rows.note: The text reports overtraining dynamics, not a second descent in test error.
rows.check: Simulations match theory; single overtraining hump, no second descent.

source_check.correct: V2 state: absent. Simulations agree with Eqs. (15) and (27), with ±2 standard deviations over 20 trials; the generalization trajectories show overtraining without a second descent.
source_check.problem: Agreement with ordinary overtraining dynamics does not establish partial epoch-wise double descent.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU student, fixed random first layer and trained output layer
rows.operation_detail: Swept the number of student hidden units and measured test error under optimal early stopping.
rows.measure: Optimal early-stopping test error versus hidden-unit count
rows.value: The text says larger models are always better in terms of early-stopping test error; the largest tested model has 16326 hidden units.
rows.uncertainty: ±1 standard error of the mean over 50 random seeds
rows.note: This reports decreasing early-stopping error with model size, but does not state a fall-rise-fall test-error curve.
rows.check: Under optimal early stopping, error falls monotonically with size and shows no peak. For V1 this is absence of the peak. For V6 it shows the peak vanishing under near-optimal regularization (early stopping approximates optimal L2, per Sec. 2.2).

source_check.correct: Split states by version: V1 absent; V6 observed for the tested early-stopping component. Optimal early-stopping test error improves with increasing model size.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Fig. 6C caption and discussion; Section 6.
source_check.problem: A single absent state misrepresents the linked V6 prediction that regularization removes the peak.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU student, fixed random first layer and trained output layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error at long training times across student sizes.
rows.measure: Long-time test error versus hidden-unit count
rows.value: The text reports that the optimal model size for long-time test error is smaller than the sample count, at approximately 60 hidden units.
rows.note: The paper does not describe a complete fall-rise-fall shape or place a second descent beyond the interpolation point.
rows.check: Text (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 6, Fig. 6F) says long-time test error diverges at Nh = P and the train-test gap drops for Nh > P. The long-time curve therefore falls, peaks at interpolation, then falls. The long-time minimum (~60 units) stays below the overparameterized branch. Upgrade from partial.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Fig. 6C–F; Section 4.2 final paragraph; Section 6 discussion following Eq. (40).
source_check.problem: The row's note understates the evidence: the text identifies divergence at interpolation and decreasing late-time train–test gap beyond it.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU student, fixed random first layer and trained output layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared overtraining across student model sizes.
rows.measure: Amount of overtraining across model complexity
rows.value: The paper reports a peak in overtraining near the point where hidden units/free parameters equal the number of samples; larger models overtrain less.
rows.note: This is a peak in overtraining amount across model sizes, not itself a reported fall-rise-fall test-error curve.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU student with both layers trained
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden-unit count while training both layers of the student.
rows.measure: Overtraining across model complexity and training dynamics
rows.value: Overtraining is transient and peaks roughly where the number of free parameters equals the number of examples; the test-error curve at that predicted peak appears to asymptote rather than diverge.
rows.note: The reported outcome concerns the overtraining peak and its behavior; it does not establish a complete test-error double-descent curve by size.
rows.check: Both layers trained: long-time test error at Nh + NiNh = P asymptotes 'much larger at the predicted peak than at other network sizes'. Long-time minimum is ≈5 hidden units. This is a model-wise peak in long-time test error, not only an overtraining measure.

source_check.problem: The row's note understates Section 4.2, which explicitly places the largest late-time error near parameter–sample equality.

rows.subject: nonlinear network on binary MNIST task, fixed random first layer
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured training and test errors during batch gradient descent.
rows.value: The text says overtraining peaks when the number of parameters matches the number of samples; it also says the peak is less distinct and less identifiable in the fixed-first-layer case.
rows.note: The authors attribute the less distinct peak to the 5000-epoch limit and maximum model size of 1740.

rows.subject: nonlinear network on binary MNIST task, both layers trained
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured training and test errors during batch gradient descent.
rows.value: The text says overtraining peaks when the number of parameters matches the number of samples; larger models outperform smaller models overall.
rows.note: The authors say the peak is less pronounced than in the longer student-teacher simulations.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU students with fixed random first layer
rows.size_stated: Nh > 300 in the overcomplete regime; largest tested Nh = 16326
rows.operation_detail: Trained the same model sizes on nearly random target labels.
rows.value: The text says overcomplete networks easily attain zero training error when trained long enough, but do not generalize well after substantial training or optimal early stopping.
rows.note: This is the low-SNR condition in the paper's comparison of noise effects.

rows.subject: nonlinear ReLU students with fixed random first layer
rows.size_stated: Nh > 300 in the overcomplete regime; largest tested Nh = 16326
rows.operation_detail: Trained the same model sizes on nearly noise-free target labels.
rows.measure: Generalization and effect of early stopping
rows.value: The text says the networks generalize well; for sufficiently large models, the benefit of early stopping nearly disappears.
rows.note: The authors contrast this with the SNR = 0.01 condition.

rows.subject: shallow linear student network
rows.size_stated: N not stated for this comparison
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimal early stopping with optimally tuned L2 regularization.
rows.value: The paper reports relative error between early stopping and optimal L2 regularization under 3 percent, with the largest discrepancy around α = 1.
